documents.title: Artificial Intelligence at NDSU: Goals, Guidance, and Research
documents.summary: Short NDSU IT page summarizing campus work-group discussions on AI: shared values, instructor and student guidance, and research needs. It says it is a framework, not formal policy, that instructors decide whether AI is allowed, and that AI contributions must be credited.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'a framework ... not a formal policy' and 'Instructors set course policies (including if AI use is allowed at all)', so the decision is delegated to instructors; no university-wide ban or permit is set.

units.why: States the page is a framework 'not a formal policy', so it sets institution-level principles and scope; P56 fits an institution-wide framework preamble.
units.anchor: a framework for how AI is approached at NDSU, not a formal policy

units.why: 'All use of AI falls under existing academic integrity, technology and other student/employee policies' binds everyone to existing policy; P77 is compliance with existing university policy.
units.anchor: All use of AI falls under existing academic integrity, technology and other student/employee policies

units.why: AI is framed as a support tool that 'should not replace critical thinking'; students remain the thinkers, so P32.
units.anchor: should not replace critical thinking

units.why: 'Instructors set course policies (including if AI use is allowed at all)' hands the decision to instructors, P04.
units.anchor: Instructors set course policies (including if AI use is allowed at all)

units.why: 'all AI contributions must be credited' is a disclosure duty for AI use; the credit/disclosure type P24 fits.
units.anchor: all AI contributions must be credited

units.why: 'Users are accountable for reliability, accuracy, and privacy (e.g., FERPA compliance)' makes users responsible for outputs; closest is P29 but it also covers privacy/FERPA.
units.anchor: Users are accountable for reliability, accuracy, and privacy
units.fit_note: Also names privacy and FERPA compliance as part of user accountability, not only ownership of submitted work.

units.why: 'AI should be discipline-specific, support personalized learning, creativity, and workforce readiness' states purpose and principles for integration; P56 framework, though it also gestures at career readiness (P44).
units.anchor: AI should be discipline-specific, support personalized learning, creativity, and workforce readiness

units.why: 'Encourage critical evaluation, not passive reliance' recommends instructors position AI as a learning partner; this is about students staying critical thinkers, P32.
units.anchor: Encourage critical evaluation, not passive reliance

units.why: 'Sample syllabus statements clarify acceptable use' points instructors to syllabus statements to communicate rules; P09 (AI statement in syllabus).
units.anchor: Sample syllabus statements clarify acceptable use aligned with NDSU policies
units.fit_note: Offers sample statements rather than requiring a syllabus statement.

units.why: 'Projects explore AI's benefits, risks, and limitations' recommends assignments built around AI; P35 redesign assignments around AI.
units.anchor: Projects explore AI’s benefits, risks, and limitations

units.why: 'Students develop prompt design, output evaluation, and AI literacy as professional competencies' ties instruction to career skill; P44.
units.anchor: prompt design, output evaluation, and AI literacy as professional competencies

units.why: 'Both instructors and students must document AI use and safeguard sensitive data' imposes a documentation duty on instructors too; P24 chosen over P47 because the duty is mutual documentation; the data-safeguarding half is coded separately as P50.
units.anchor: Both instructors and students must document AI use
units.fit_note: Binds instructors as well as students to document their AI use.

units.why: Second half of the same bullet: 'safeguard sensitive data' is a data-protection duty, P50.
units.anchor: safeguard sensitive data

units.why: 'Misuse violates academic honesty' classifies AI misuse as an integrity violation, P36.
units.anchor: Misuse violates academic honesty

units.why: 'Check Instructor Expectations: Policies differ by course' tells students to check each instructor's rules; P10 ask/check before using, P11 also relevant but the action is checking.
units.anchor: Check Instructor Expectations: Policies differ by course

units.why: 'Cite or explain AI use in assignments' is a student disclosure duty, P24.
units.anchor: Cite or explain AI use in assignments

units.why: 'AI should support—not replace—independent thought' keeps students as the thinkers, P32.
units.anchor: AI should support—not replace—independent thought

units.why: 'Always fact-check outputs' under bias awareness tells students to verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: Always fact-check outputs

units.why: 'Protect personal data and respect copyright' covers privacy and IP; the data half is P50 and copyright P52; one unit is allowed so P50 is the lead and the note records IP.
units.anchor: Protect personal data and respect copyright
units.fit_note: Also requires respecting copyright (P52), not only protecting personal data.

units.why: 'AI Fluency: Tool selection, prompt writing, bias evaluation, and adaptability' names AI skills for students as professional competence, P44.
units.anchor: AI Fluency: Tool selection, prompt writing, bias evaluation, and adaptability

units.why: The research summary reports 62+ research groups and names needs such as HPC; this is an institutional status assessment of research AI capacity, not a rule on teaching, so no type fits well.
units.anchor: NDSU supports 62+ research groups using AI across all colleges
units.uncovered_note: Institutional status and needs assessment of AI research capacity (groups, GPUs, centralized AI center), not a rule on AI use in teaching.

units.why: Lists needs including 'a centralized AI strategy/center', an institutional plan for AI governance; P56 fits framework/strategy.
units.anchor: a centralized AI strategy/center
units.fit_note: Identifies a need for a strategy or center rather than stating a principle.

documents.title: AI in the Classroom: An NDSU Instructor Guide
documents.summary: A ChatGPT-assisted guide for NDSU instructors that urges clear expectations, transparency, AI skepticism, and AI literacy, with sample syllabus statements, assignments and a suspected-misuse process. It leaves the rule to each instructor and offers examples ranging from permitted-with-credit to no AI for a literature review.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'Some instructors may encourage AI for brainstorming and revision, while others may prohibit its use altogether' and offers sample statements rather than a single rule, so stance is delegates.

units.why: Introduction says instructors 'have a responsibility for their own use of AI' and shape students' use; defines the instructors' role, P59 closest as it concerns instructors' own AI conduct, though no specific use is named.
units.anchor: instructors at North Dakota State University (NDSU) have a responsibility for their own use of
units.fit_note: States a general responsibility for instructors' own AI use without naming particular uses.

units.why: Says AI 'has the potential to enhance learning' and prepare students for work; a rationale tying AI to careers, P44.
units.anchor: prepare students for a workforce increasingly reliant on digital tools

units.why: Says instructors 'have the opportunity to model effective and ethical AI use'; a recommendation about instructors' own AI use as modeling, P59.
units.anchor: Instructors have the opportunity to model effective and ethical AI use
units.fit_note: Frames instructor AI use as modeling for students.

units.why: The guide discloses 'produced by iterative prompting, selecting, and adapting of outputs from Chat-GPT'; an institutional disclosure of AI-made materials, P48.
units.anchor: produced by iterative prompting, selecting, and adapting of outputs from Chat-GPT
units.fit_note: Discloses that the guide itself was AI-drafted; does not state that it was reviewed.

units.why: 'Position AI as a learning tool, not a replacement' says AI should support outcomes; AI must not replace students' thinking, P32.
units.anchor: AI should support learning and progress towards learning outcomes

units.why: 'Over-reliance on AI can weaken students' problem-solving and communication skills' explains that AI shortcuts skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: Over-reliance on AI can weaken students’ problem-solving and communication skills

units.why: 'Encouraging students to use AI as a tool for collaboration and inquiry' recommends AI use by default for inquiry; P02 permit/encourage.
units.anchor: Encouraging students to use AI as a tool for collaboration and inquiry

units.why: Instructor Tip asks for tasks where students 'engage with AI critically', such as comparing outputs or revising them; assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Assign tasks that require students to engage with AI critically

units.why: The sample assignment has students 'experiment with a tool (e.g., ChatGPT, WolframAlpha, GitHub Copilot)', generate code and reflect; an assignment built around AI use, P35.
units.anchor: experiment with a tool (e.g., ChatGPT, WolframAlpha, GitHub Copilot), and reflect on their experience

units.why: Assignment component asks students to 'Document: What you asked the AI; What it produced; How you evaluated its accuracy', a prompt/output record; P26 transcripts/logs.
units.anchor: What you asked the AI
units.fit_note: Applies to a sample assignment, recording prompt, output and accuracy evaluation.

units.why: Reflection essay asks how AI 'helped or hindered your work' and what ethical principles guided use; a reflection on AI use, P26.
units.anchor: Discuss how the AI helped or hindered your work

units.why: Class debate on 'Should AI be allowed in academic work in our field?' and students 'propose guidelines'; instructors co-create guidelines with students, P67.
units.anchor: Encourage students to propose guidelines for ethical AI use
units.fit_note: Part of a sample debate assignment rather than a stated policy-setting process.

units.why: 'NDSU has policies that address responsible AI use' and instructors 'should familiarize themselves'; P77 compliance with existing university policy.
units.anchor: Instructors should familiarize themselves with these policies

units.why: 'Students may misuse AI by submitting AI-generated work as their own' defines misuse, P19 (AI should not produce submitted work).
units.anchor: Students may misuse AI by submitting

units.why: Same sentence names 'failing to critically engage with AI-generated content' as misuse; this is verifying and evaluating output, P31.
units.anchor: failing to critically engage with AI-generated content

units.why: 'Clearly defining what constitutes acceptable AI use in coursework' is an instruction to instructors to state expectations; P09.
units.anchor: Clearly defining what constitutes acceptable AI use in coursework
units.fit_note: Phrased as a benefit and good practice, not a mandate.

units.why: 'A good classroom policy provides guardrails without inhibiting creativity' states a design principle for course policies; no type fits it, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: A good classroom policy provides guardrails without inhibiting creativity
units.uncovered_note: A design principle for course AI policies: guardrails without inhibiting creativity.

units.why: Instructor Tip: 'Include a statement in your syllabus about AI use, specifying whether, when, and how' is a syllabus statement recommendation, P09.
units.anchor: Include a statement in your syllabus about AI use

units.why: Sample syllabus statement: 'All writing submitted for any course must be produced by the student', a rule that students produce their own writing, P19.
units.anchor: All writing submitted for any course must be produced by the student
units.fit_note: Prose-specific rule; AI is not mentioned in this sentence.

units.why: Sample statement: 'We will also discuss the role of AI in writing processes', the instructor commits to discuss AI in class, P66.
units.anchor: We will also discuss the role of AI in writing processes

units.why: Sample statement: AI composition 'submitted as the student's own writing without acknowledging the role that AI played ... violates the writing program's academic integrity policy'; nondisclosure is the violation, P28 chosen over P36 because the violation hinges on lack of acknowledgment.
units.anchor: submitted as the student’s own writing without acknowledging the role that AI played

units.why: Sample statement: writing not produced by the student 'without attribution, whether it was written by a human or AI, is a violation ... subject to disciplinary action'; AI treated like any other source, P45.
units.anchor: whether it was written by a human or AI, is a violation of the university’s

units.why: Sample statement says students found guilty face 'penalties, up to and possibly including suspension and/or expulsion'; concrete penalty range, P37.
units.anchor: subject to penalties, up to and possibly including suspension and/or expulsion

units.why: Sample statement says work 'must adhere to the Code of Academic Responsibility and Conduct'; compliance with existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: Work submitted in all courses must adhere to the Code of Academic Responsibility and Conduct

units.why: Program policy example 1 (from Duke): 'Students are allowed to use advanced automated tools ... if that use is properly documented and credited'; permit with disclosure, P02 as the default permit; the disclosure part is coded in the next units.
units.anchor: Students are allowed to use advanced automated tools
units.fit_note: Permission is conditional on documentation and credit.

units.why: The Duke example gives a citation format with the query text, date and tool; cite tool, prompt and date, P25.
units.anchor: Text of your query.
units.fit_note: Anchor is a fragment of the citation template; the full template names tool, date of query and query text.

units.why: Duke example: 'Material generated using other tools should follow a similar citation convention'; extends citation to all tools, P24.
units.anchor: Material generated using other tools should follow a similar citation convention

units.why: NDSU Center for Writers example: instructors 'try to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate plagiarism, as well as whether and how AI has been used'; an evidentiary distinction, P69.
units.anchor: try to distinguish between inadvertent and deliberate plagiarism, as well as whether and how AI
units.fit_note: Distinguishes kinds of misuse and intent rather than setting an evidence standard.

units.why: 'Deliberate plagiarism may result in zero for the assignment, possibly an F for the course' is a stated penalty, P37.
units.anchor: Deliberate plagiarism may result in zero for the assignment, possibly an F for the course
units.fit_note: Penalty is stated for plagiarism generally.

units.why: For AI text in an assignment where AI was not allowed: 'Initial instances will be discussed in a meeting with the instructor, and revision will be required'; first offense handled educatively with a meeting and rewrite, P68.
units.anchor: Initial instances will be discussed in a meeting with the instructor, and revision will be
units.fit_note: Combines a meeting and a mandatory rewrite for a first AI-misuse instance.

units.why: 'Repeated instances may result in zero for the assignment, possibly an F for the course' states an escalating penalty for repeat AI misuse, P37.
units.anchor: Repeated instances may result in zero for the assignment, possibly an F for the course

units.why: The example treats AI text where 'AI was not included as part of the assignment' as a violation; AI is barred unless the assignment includes it, P06 fallback rule.
units.anchor: an assignment in which AI was not included as part of the assignment
units.fit_note: Implied rather than explicit: the penalty applies only where AI was not part of the assignment.

units.why: Suspected plagiarism process: instructors may consider 'evidence of engaging in the writing process'; evidence to weigh, P69.
units.anchor: look for evidence of engaging in the writing process

units.why: Advises that 'plugging an assignment prompt into ChatGPT can result in text that is quite close to what a student submitted', a detection technique, P40.
units.anchor: plugging an assignment prompt into ChatGPT can result in text that is quite close to

units.why: TurnItIn 'can be problematic because it collects student writing' and presents results 'with little context'; caution on similarity checkers, P40 closest as it discusses a similarity check tool.
units.anchor: this software can be problematic because it collects student writing
units.fit_note: Tool is offered but flagged as problematic; the unit cautions rather than endorses.

units.why: 'asking ChatGPT if a text was written by it does not produce accurate/reliable results' says AI self-detection is unreliable, P39.
units.anchor: does not produce accurate/reliable results

units.why: 'FERPA guidelines prohibit us from inputting student writing into an AI tool without a student's permission' restricts instructors' data use, P50.
units.anchor: FERPA guidelines prohibit us from inputting student writing into an AI tool without a student’s

units.why: Process step 1: students misuse AI 'in times of stress ... or when they do not understand an assignment'; presume good faith, P68.
units.anchor: they choose these options in times of stress, when they feel overwhelmed

units.why: Process steps 2-3: 'Reach out to the student via email and request a meeting' and discuss process, P57 talk before escalating.
units.anchor: Reach out to the student via email and request a meeting

units.why: Step 3 lists questions to ask: have them 'summarize what they wrote' and describe tools used; a conversation that checks understanding, P34.
units.anchor: ask them to summarize what they wrote
units.fit_note: Used as a misconduct inquiry, not a routine assessment.

units.why: Step 5: 'If they dispute this, ask them to provide you with evidence of their process (i.e. multiple drafts, brainstorming)'; a chance to respond with evidence, P64.
units.anchor: If they dispute this, ask them to provide you with evidence of their process

units.why: Step 6: 'If it's a first-time problem, provide the student with an opportunity to rewrite/revise', an educative first-offense response, P68.
units.anchor: provide the student with an opportunity to rewrite/revise the assignment

units.why: Step 7: 'Report it as a case of academic misconduct (this provides students the opportunity to appeal)', routing to integrity process with appeal, P36.
units.anchor: Report it as a case of academic misconduct
units.fit_note: Also notes students may appeal, which touches P64.

units.why: 'Some instructors may encourage AI for brainstorming and revision, while others may prohibit its use altogether' describes per-instructor variation, P04.
units.anchor: Some instructors may encourage AI for brainstorming and revision, while others may prohibit its use

units.why: 'Providing explicit guidance in syllabi and assignment instructions helps students navigate these differences', P09.
units.anchor: Providing explicit guidance in syllabi and assignment instructions

units.why: Tip: 'Discuss AI policies early in the semester' asks instructors to explain rules to students, P66.
units.anchor: Discuss AI policies early in the semester

units.why: Tip: 'include an AI use section on all assignment instructions, and provide examples of acceptable and unacceptable use', P09 per-assignment statement.
units.anchor: include an “AI use” section on all assignment instructions

units.why: Sample use statement: 'None of your literature review may be written by AI text generators ... and used as if it were your own work', P19 for prose.
units.anchor: None of your literature review may be written by AI text generators

units.why: Gives reason: AI 'can hallucinate sources and often contains inaccuracies'; AI output unreliable, P31.
units.anchor: AI is not consistently reliable or effective at literature reviews

units.why: 'Suspected AI plagiarism will necessitate a meeting with me and a conversation about your writing process' states the response in advance; talk before escalating, P57.
units.anchor: Suspected AI plagiarism will necessitate a meeting with me

units.why: 'Only an acceptably re-written paper will receive a grade' states the concrete consequence in advance, P37.
units.anchor: Only an acceptably re-written paper will receive a grade

units.why: 'Generative AI may be used productively as a thinking partner to brainstorm topics and narrow the scope of your research question', P15.
units.anchor: Generative AI may be used productively as a thinking partner to brainstorm topics

units.why: AI 'may also be used as a supplement to peer review' with the prompt 'do not re-write it for me', permitted feedback use for prose, P18.
units.anchor: It may also be used as a supplement to peer review
units.fit_note: Requires a prompt that stops the AI from rewriting; also involves giving AI the draft.

units.why: 'If generative AI is used ... you must include transparent evidence and explanation for how it was used in your final author's note', P24.
units.anchor: you must include transparent evidence and explanation for how it was used

units.why: Section 4 tells instructors to 'guide students toward responsible, transparent use' if AI helps meet objectives, P24 framed for instructors.
units.anchor: instructors should guide students toward responsible, transparent use

units.why: 'they should clearly communicate how they used it—whether through citations, reflective statements, or assignment-specific disclosure', P24.
units.anchor: they should clearly communicate how they used it

units.why: Explains disclosure 'mirrors real-world expectations, as many industries require professionals to document AI-assisted work', a career rationale, P44.
units.anchor: many industries require professionals to document AI-assisted work

units.why: Tip: 'Require students to explain how they used AI in an assignment', P24 (explanation as disclosure).
units.anchor: Require students to explain how they used AI in an assignment

units.why: Sample self-assessment memo requires a one-page reflective memo on 'use of digital tools (including AI)', P26.
units.anchor: must also include a one-page, single-spaced reflective memo

units.why: Section 5: AI 'can generate inaccurate, outdated, or biased content, making it essential for students to critically evaluate AI-generated outputs', P31.
units.anchor: essential for students to critically evaluate AI-generated outputs

units.why: 'students should learn to verify AI-generated information against credible sources', P31.
units.anchor: students should learn to verify AI-generated information against credible sources

units.why: Tip: 'Incorporate discussions about AI biases and misinformation into research-based assignments', P53 bias concerns, as an instructor teaching move.
units.anchor: Incorporate discussions about AI biases and misinformation into research-based assignments
units.fit_note: Directs instructors to teach about bias, rather than naming harms directly.

units.why: Tip: 'Assign students to generate and critique AI-generated bibliographies', an assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Assign students to generate and critique AI-generated bibliographies

units.why: Sample reflective memo: 'AI text generators cannot be used to write your literature review without violating the principles of academic honesty and program policy', P19.
units.anchor: AI text generators cannot be used to write your literature review

units.why: The memo assignment has students 'After your literature review is written, experiment' by asking AI to complete it; permitted experimentation in a later step, P08 staged permission.
units.anchor: After your literature review is written, experiment with the following
units.fit_note: Permission to use AI follows the human-written review within one assignment, not across a course.

units.why: Memo asks students to 'Keep careful record and observational notes about your prompts', P26.
units.anchor: Keep careful record and observational notes about your prompts

units.why: 'Attachments: please include your complete outputs' requires submitting AI outputs, P26.
units.anchor: please include your complete outputs

units.why: Section 6: 'Some platforms retain user input, which could violate FERPA' notes tools retain input and FERPA risk, P50.
units.anchor: Some platforms retain user input, which could violate FERPA

units.why: 'using AI responsibly means protecting personal data and respecting intellectual property', P50.
units.anchor: Instructors should help students understand that using AI responsibly means protecting personal data

units.why: Tip: 'Warn students about inputting sensitive or protected information into AI platforms', P50.

units.why: Tip: 'discuss the legal and ethical considerations around AI-generated content', P52 licensing/copyright and ethics.
units.anchor: discuss the legal and ethical considerations around

units.why: Section 7: instructors 'can integrate AI literacy into courses by teaching students' tool choice, prompting, evaluation; P44 teaching AI use as a professional skill.
units.anchor: instructors can integrate AI literacy into courses

units.why: 'Help students learn when to use AI for research, writing, data analysis, coding, or creative ideation', P44.
units.anchor: Help students learn when to use AI for research, writing, data analysis, coding, or creative

units.why: 'Encourage students to refine their prompts for more accurate and useful responses', teaching prompt skill, P44.
units.anchor: Encourage students to refine their prompts for more accurate and useful responses

units.why: 'AI content should always be assessed for accuracy, bias, and appropriateness', P31.
units.anchor: AI content should always be assessed for accuracy, bias, and appropriateness

units.why: 'Design assignments that require students to critique, expand, or refine AI-generated work rather than passively accepting it', P35.

units.why: 'human judgment, creativity, and ethical reasoning remain essential', students stay the thinkers, P32.

documents.title: Using AI Effectively and Responsibly: A Guide for Students
documents.summary: A student-facing guide urging compliance with university policy, checking each instructor's rules, transparency about AI use, treating AI as a tool and verifying outputs. It sets no rule itself and defers to instructors.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'AI policies can vary by course and instructor' and 'Always review your syllabus and ask for clarification', deferring to instructors instead of setting a stance.

units.why: Introduction says the guide offers 'practical recommendations for using AI in ways that support learning, uphold academic integrity'; framing of purpose, P56.
units.anchor: practical recommendations for using AI in ways that support learning, uphold academic integrity

units.why: Student guide discloses it was produced from Chat-GPT and Co-Pilot output; disclosure of AI-made materials, P48.
units.anchor: produced by iterative prompting, selecting, and adapting of outputs from Chat-GPT and Co-Pilot
units.fit_note: Discloses AI drafting but not review.

units.why: 'approaching AI responsibly ... build technological fluency, and contribute more productively to the region's workforce' ties AI use to career, P44.
units.anchor: build technological fluency, and contribute more productively

units.why: 'Before using AI tools, familiarize yourself with university guidelines' is a compliance duty, P77.
units.anchor: Before using AI tools, familiarize yourself with university guidelines

units.why: 'Misuse of AI-generated content—such as submitting AI-written work as your own—could violate academic honesty rules', P19 with misconduct.
units.anchor: submitting AI-written work as your own—could violate academic honesty rules
units.fit_note: Phrased as 'could violate' rather than a flat ban; classification as misconduct (P36) also present.

units.why: 'AI policies can vary by course and instructor ... Always review your syllabus and ask for clarification before using AI', P10.
units.anchor: Always review your syllabus and ask for clarification before using AI in assignments

units.why: 'Some professors may encourage AI for brainstorming or revising, while others may prohibit its use' describes instructor-level variation, P04.
units.anchor: AI policies can vary by course and instructor

units.why: 'Learning to navigate different instructor expectations mirrors what you will encounter in the workplace' gives a career rationale, P44.
units.anchor: Learning to navigate different instructor expectations mirrors what you will encounter in the workplace

units.why: Learner Tip: 'Treat AI like a study partner, not a substitute for your own work', P32.
units.anchor: Treat AI like a study partner, not a substitute for your own work
units.fit_note: Also frames AI as a study partner (P12).

units.why: 'If you use AI to assist with research, writing, or idea generation, clearly communicate how and to what extent you used it', P24.
units.anchor: clearly communicate how and to what extent you used it

units.why: Disclosure can be 'citing AI-generated content, providing a brief explanation with your assignment, or following the instructor's disclosure requirements', P24, with the instructor deciding the form.
units.anchor: citing AI-generated content, providing a brief explanation with your assignment

units.why: 'many industries require employees to document AI-assisted work' gives a professional rationale for disclosure, P44.
units.anchor: many industries require employees to document AI-assisted work

units.why: Learner Tip: 'Use AI as a starting point, not a final product', P32.
units.anchor: Use AI as a starting point, not a final product

units.why: 'it should never replace critical thinking, creativity, or personal expertise', P32.
units.anchor: it should never replace critical thinking, creativity, or personal expertise

units.why: 'Relying too heavily on AI outputs can weaken your ability to develop essential communication and problem-solving skills', P41.
units.anchor: Relying too heavily on AI outputs can weaken your ability to develop essential communication and

units.anchor: The workforce will require professionals who can collaborate with AI

units.why: 'If you can simply be replaced by AI work, what is your value to employers?' warns students about replaceability; career rationale, P44.
units.anchor: If you can simply be replaced by AI work, what is your value to employers?

units.why: 'AI ... cannot be relied on without questioning and confirming. It can produce incorrect, outdated, hallucinated, or biased information', P31.
units.anchor: cannot be relied on without questioning and confirming

units.why: 'always check AI-generated content against credible sources, especially when working with research, data, or citations', P31.
units.anchor: always check AI-generated content against credible sources

units.why: 'At NDSU, uncritical use of AI may result in violation of academic integrity', links unverified use to misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: uncritical use of AI may result in violation of academic integrity

units.why: 'Developing AI skepticism now will prepare you to be a responsible, informed user', P44.
units.anchor: Developing AI skepticism now will prepare you to be a responsible, informed user

units.why: 'Avoid sharing your own or other peoples' personal data and work, as some AI platforms may store or use that information', P50 with a P49 element on others' work.
units.anchor: Avoid sharing your own or other peoples’ personal data and work

units.why: 'most generative AI is based on internet content that includes copyrighted material' notes IP concern, P52.

units.why: 'intellectual property and data security laws govern AI use, and mishandling protected information can have serious consequences', P77 compliance with law.
